records.question: Based on Figure 1, the method description, and Tables 1 and 2, which design choices appear most important for humor prediction?
records.answer:
The proposed framework uses an LSTM to model the dialogue sequence, which the paper presents as a first-ever LSTM application to humor response prediction.
Figure 1 shows three CNN input features (words, word2vec, character trigrams) feeding an utterance encoding layer, whose high-level feature vectors go into an LSTM and then a softmax layer.
Table 1 shows LSTM + high level features gives the best results (Accuracy 70.0, F-score 62.9), better than CRF variants and plain LSTM.
Table 2 shows CNN sentence encoding outperforms LSTM sentence encoding (70.0 vs 68.4 accuracy; 62.9 vs 59.1 F1).
Earlier bag-of-ngram or simple RNN approaches were found not ideal for capturing setup context, motivating the LSTM design.

query_analysis.interpretation: The figure shows a design where each utterance is processed by three parallel CNNs (one per input feature: words, word2vec, character trigrams), producing high-level feature vectors (l_t) which are then fed into an LSTM for temporal modeling across utterance tokens, followed by a softmax layer for classification (y_t). The architecture is modular, with clear separation of input encoding (CNN), sequential modeling (LSTM), and output prediction (softmax).

metadata.nearby_text: the same high level feature vector added at the end of the neural network, 1-2-3gram features of a win- dow made by the utterance and the four previous, and the two feature sets combined. We also com- pared the overall system where we replace the CNN with an LSTM sentence encoder (Li et al., 2015), where we kept the same input features. In the neural network we set the size to 100 for all the hidden layers of the CNN and the LSTM, and 5 to the convolutional window. A CNN-LSTM network seems to over- come this issue as the CNN stage is better in model- ing the lexical and semantic content of the utterance, as the LSTM allows to put each utterance in relation with the past context, ﬁltering out many false posi- tives from wrong contexts. We applied a dropout regularization layer (Srivastava et al., 2014) after the output of the LSTM, and L2 regularization on the softmax output layer. The choice of the CNN is further justiﬁed by the results obtained from the comparison between the CNN and the LSTM sentence encoding input, shown in table 2. We may consider in the future to use more data, and try other sentence input encoders, including deeper or bi-directional LSTMs, to ﬁnd the most effective one. As a baseline for comparison we used an imple- mentation of the Conditional Random Field (Laf- ferty et al., 2001) from CRFSuite (Okazaki, 2007), with L2 regularization.
